title: Government and Industry Join Forces as One Team to Enter the Global Civil Aircraft Market
text:
– KASA Launches Public-Private Joint Task Force for International Joint Development of Civil Aircraft– Supporting Korean Companies’ Entry into Global Supply Chains and Participation in International Joint Development Projects
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) held the kickoff meeting of the “Public-Private Joint Task Force for International Joint Development of Civil Aircraft” (hereinafter referred to as the “Task Force”) on July 16 (Thu) at the Seoul Central Post Office, with participation from relevant government ministries and aircraft manufacturing companies.
The meeting was attended by officials from relevant ministries and agencies, including the Presidential Office, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, the Ministry of SMEs and Startups, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Financial Services Commission, as well as representatives from industry, including Korea Aerospace Industries, Korean Air, and Hanwha Aerospace.
The Task Force was established to lay the foundation for Korean companies’ participation in international joint development projects for next-generation civil aircraft and to establish a cooperative framework through which the government and industry can jointly respond.
The next-generation civil aircraft international joint development project aims to enable Korean companies to participate as key partners in next-generation civil aircraft development programs led by global aircraft manufacturers such as Airbus and Boeing.
Specifically, as these global civil aircraft manufacturers develop new aircraft models to replace existing models such as the A320 and Boeing 737, Korean companies will take the lead in developing key components or modules and secure exclusive supply rights for those items over the long term during the mass production phase.
Although significant costs and efforts are required for Korean companies to independently develop these items, the project is essential for domestic aircraft manufacturers, as successful development would enable them to stably export the relevant products for at least 20 to 30 years.
In addition, the project holds significant importance in terms of securing early access to technologies for developing next-generation aircraft with significantly lower fuel consumption and maximized production efficiency compared with existing aircraft, as well as advanced engine technologies.
The development of next-generation civil aircraft is expected to begin in earnest around 2030. Given the characteristics of the aviation industry, which requires enormous development costs and extensive periods of time, thorough preparation and investment are needed from now.
In this regard, President Lee Jae Myung emphasized the importance of this project at the 5th National Space Committee meeting on July 3 and instructed the prompt establishment of a dedicated organization to consolidate government-wide capabilities.
The Task Force will be headed by Administrator Taeseog Oh of KASA, with director-general-level officials from relevant ministries participating as members. It will also include up to approximately 100 domestic companies, relevant associations, and external experts.
Going forward, the Task Force will seek government-wide support measures, including strengthening the technological capabilities of domestic companies, expanding production facilities, and securing stable investment funding. It will also play a role in enhancing negotiation capabilities by establishing an organic cooperation system among domestic companies.
In addition, KASA plans to closely cooperate with local governments, academia, and research institutes to discuss various support measures, including securing specialized talent and linking with balanced regional development policies.
Jouhahn Lee, Presidential Secretary for Science and Technology Policy, stated, “This initiative represents an important opportunity to expand the growth foundation of Korea’s aircraft manufacturing industry and increase the possibility of domestic companies entering global supply chains,” emphasizing the need for close cooperation among relevant ministries and industry.
Administrator Taeseog Oh of KASA stated, “Participation in international joint development projects for civil aircraft marks an important turning point for Korea’s aircraft manufacturing industry to move beyond simple parts supply and secure high value-added manufacturing capabilities.” He added, “KASA will bring together the capabilities of the government and industry centered around the Task Force and actively support Korean companies in establishing themselves as key players in the global civil aircraft manufacturing supply chain.”

title: Expanding the Path for Future Space Cooperation with Saudi Arabia
text:
– Meeting with Governor of Saudi Arabia’s Communications, Space & Technology Commission; Discussions Held on Space Cooperation
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) met with Governor Haitham AlOhali of the Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST) of Saudi Arabia (a Board Member of the Saudi Space Agency) on July 15 (Wed) at the Government Complex Seoul to discuss space cooperation between Korea and Saudi Arabia.
The meeting was held to share the current status of space cooperation between the two countries and explore ways to expand practical and multifaceted partnerships toward jointly opening a new era of the space economy.
In particular, both sides highlighted the space education program titled “KAIST Summer School Invitation Program for Talent Development” for Saudi university students being conducted for 3 weeks by KASA in cooperation with the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), and agreed to build networks among future generations in the space sector and further expand bilateral space cooperation through the program.
In addition, Administrator Oh of KASA highlighted the growing momentum for investment in new space industries in Saudi Arabia under its “Vision 2030” initiative and proposed establishing business connections to support the smooth entry of Korean space companies with advanced technological capabilities into Saudi Arabia’s space economy market.
Administrator Oh stated, “We will diversify space cooperation with Saudi Arabia and further strengthen our partnership,” adding, “Building on government-to-government channels, we will actively support Korean space companies in expanding overseas and achieving tangible results in the Middle Eastern market.”

title: Building an Irreplaceable South Korea for All,Powered by AI and Science & Technology
text:
– 2026 Second-Half Work Plan Report by MSIT and KASA
[Key Focus Areas]
① Full-Scale Implementation of the Three Mega Projects
② Realizing an AI Basic Society Accessible to All
③ Building a Science and Technology Ecosystem that Strives for Global Excellence
④ Building Growth Pathways for Youth and Supporting Regional Innovation Growth
⑤ Advancing Toward Becoming One of the World’s Top Five Aerospace Powers
The Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister Bae Kyung-hoon) and the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) reported their 2026 second-half work plans to the President at the Blue House on July 16 (Thu).
This work plan report was the second presidentially chaired report since the launch of the new administration. During the meeting, the government closely reviewed whether the policies and pending issues reported last December had been implemented without disruption, and held in-depth discussions on key tasks to be pursued in the second half of 2026.
Under the vision of “An Irreplaceable South Korea for All, Powered by AI and Science & Technology,” MSIT established five key focus areas for the second half of 2026: full-scale implementation of the three mega projects, realizing an AI basic society accessible to all, building a science and technology ecosystem that strives for global excellence, building growth pathways for youth and supporting regional innovation growth, and advancing toward becoming one of the world’s top five aerospace powers, and formulated key initiatives accordingly.
Korea will secure world-class capabilities in AI data centers, Physical AI, and semiconductors, taking a great leap forward as an irreplaceable nation.
– Developing AI Data Centers into a National Strategic Industry
The government will support the smooth operation of gigawatt-scale super-large AI data centers, which will be built through approximately KRW 550 trillion in private investment from companies including SK, GS, and Naver. A three-pillar support system consisting of a pan-government task force, a public-private alliance, and a dedicated support team will facilitate the prompt implementation of administrative procedures required by companies, including securing electricity and sites and obtaining necessary approvals.
Starting next year, the government will promote the localization and advancement of key solutions and equipment for AI data centers, including IT, power, and cooling systems. In connection with cluster development, it will also provide comprehensive support packages covering talent development, test labs, finance, and exports to foster related industries.
– Securing World-Class Competitiveness in Physical AI
Physical AI is an area where Korea, with its strong industrial infrastructure and world-class AI capabilities, can excel, and the government aims to become the global No. 1 by 2030.
To secure high-quality data combining physical laws and movements, Korea will begin developing its own world model capable of mass-producing physics-based synthetic data this year. Based on accumulated data, the government will establish a system for learning and training Physical AI and secure a world-class Physical AI foundation model within the next three years, ultimately completing a homegrown Physical AI full-stack ecosystem. The government will also conduct leading demonstration projects applying these technological achievements not only in manufacturing sites but also in various fields, including national defense, caregiving, and agriculture, and foster Physical AI as an export industry.
– K-Semiconductor: Strengthening Korea’s Super-Gap Competitiveness
The government will establish a comprehensive Korean AI semiconductor ecosystem encompassing AI semiconductor chips, infrastructure and networks, software, and services, all developed domestically. It will also expand support measures to help the ecosystem establish an early foothold in the market, including facilitating the adoption of products by major companies and supporting public-led procurement of innovative products.
To secure next-generation semiconductor source technologies, the government plans to begin, following preliminary planning in the second half of this year, developing semiconductors that can overcome the current physical limitations such as ultra-fine (1nm-class devices) and stacked next-generation HBM semiconductors.
② Realizing an AI Basic Society Accessible to All
The government will create an environment where all citizens can easily and affordably utilize Korean AI services, ensuring that differences in access to and capabilities for using AI do not lead to economic and social disparities.
– Launching “AI for All” Services Accessible to All Citizens
Within this year, the government plans to provide citizens with a general-purpose AI chatbot service, similar to ChatGPT, based on domestic AI models without cost burdens or usage limitations. The service will also include AI-based assistance that helps citizens easily find and apply for various government support benefits, such as youth subsidies, by providing information and completing application procedures on their behalf.
Starting next year, the government will further advance the service into more accessible AI agents, ushering in an era of one AI agent per person nationwide.
– Securing Globally Top-Tier Homegrown AI Models
As the importance of securing independent AI models grows amid U.S. restrictions on AI access, Korea will secure an AI model ranking among the global top 10 by the second half of this year. The government will then focus on securing globally top-tier homegrown AI models through bold and intensive support for advanced GPUs, data, and talent.
– Enabling Everyone to Use AI in Daily Life
The government will also strengthen AI utilization education for all citizens. In cooperation with 12 relevant ministries, including MSIT, the Ministry of Education, and the Ministry of Employment and Labor, the government will provide AI education opportunities to 5.14 million people within this year. Starting in the second half of this year, the government will establish an online education environment where citizens can easily find and take AI courses offered by both the private and public sectors in one place, while expanding outreach education programs for senior citizens and vulnerable groups to further improve accessibility.
AI services closely related to people’s daily lives will also be launched within this year. Beginning with four services in the second half of this year — agricultural and livestock product price comparisons, AI tax consultation, national heritage interpretation, and child and youth crisis response on social media — a total of 10 services will be launched by next year.
– Creating a Safe AI-Powered Daily Life
To protect citizens’ valuable assets and information from cyber threats caused by AI, the government began vulnerability assessments in July using cutting-edge AI technologies targeting infrastructure in areas closely related to people’s daily lives and safety, including telecommunications and platforms. In addition, the government plans to develop and distribute security-specialized AI models based on Korea’s own homegrown AI models.
The government will accelerate the advancement of strategic technologies to lead the global technology competition and secure Super-Gap growth engines.
– Addressing National Challenges by Integrating Strategic Technologies with AI
The government will accelerate the implementation of the K-Moonshot initiative, which aims to address national challenges by integrating and utilizing AI in strategic technology research. In the quantum sector, Korea aims to secure a domestically developed 50-qubit quantum computer within this year and develop a 100-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The government also plans to designate quantum clusters and actively support the discovery and expansion of region-based use cases for quantum technologies.
In new drug development, an autonomous experimentation infrastructure is being established from April this year for the rapid verification of AI-designed drug candidates using AI and robots. Korea will begin developing a cancer-specific AI model in 2027 and unveil an initial model by the end of 2028, shortening the drug development period.
Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology, which enables computers to be controlled through brain signals, aims to demonstrate products for patients with paralysis by 2030. To this end, an industry-academia-research-medical BCI council will be launched in August this year, followed by the development of fundamental technologies, including AI capable of interpreting and translating signals between the brain and computers, beginning next year.
– Securing World’s First and Leading Technologies to Drive the Energy Transition
In preparation for increasing electricity demand in the AI era, the government will promote technological innovation in small modular reactors (SMRs) and nuclear fusion. Alongside the ongoing construction of Korea’s first commercial SMR facility by 2035, the government will announce a strategy for developing next-generation SMRs including molten salt reactors and micro modular reactors in July. Next year, Korea will launch a large-scale public-private partnership project to construct nuclear-powered vessels equipped with SMRs.
In the field of nuclear fusion, Korea is currently conducting the design of a demonstration reactor with the goal of realizing electricity generation in the 2030s. Starting next year, the government plans to establish public-private cooperation models, including special purpose companies (SPCs), to complete the demonstration reactor by 2035.
The government will also transition to a national R&D system that maximizes researchers’ willingness to take on challenges and pursue innovation. It will remove obstacles that hinder innovation and immersion throughout the entire R&D process and implement institutional improvements to maximize researchers’ creativity and spirit of challenge.
– Creating an Environment Where Researchers Can Focus Solely on Research
The government will introduce a system for “turning failures into assets” to encourage researchers to take bold challenges without fear of failure. Through an amendment to the Enforcement Decree of the National R&D Innovation Act scheduled for July this year, a system will be established to allow researchers to receive support for follow-up research even when research goals are not achieved, provided that the research process was meaningful.
The government will also promote the integration and linkage of information systems to reduce researchers’ administrative burdens. Research institution systems and the Integrated R&D Information System (IRIS) will be connected, resolving the inconvenience of having to enter duplicate information into both systems. Major research support systems such as IRIS (for project content), Ezbaro and RCMS (for funds), and NTIS (for performance disclosure) that are currently separated will be integrated by 2028.
A new “investment-based R&D” model, in which the government shares risks in emerging technology fields where private investment is difficult, will be introduced, enabling a virtuous cycle of recovery and reinvestment when investments succeed. The government plans to establish a legal foundation within 2026 and launch pilot projects from 2027.
– Innovating Research Methods and R&D Management Systems Through AI
The government will expand AI infrastructure to improve research productivity. Supercomputer No. 6 will be launched in September to provide researchers with advanced GPUs in a timely manner. The government will also establish subordinate regulations under the Research Data Act (effective June 2027) to enable the full sharing and utilization of all research data, except for data related to national security or corporate trade secrets.
AI will also be introduced into research administration by the government in R&D management processes, including selecting evaluation committee members, monitoring research funds, and interpreting R&D-related regulations, to enhance fairness and reliability.
– Enhancing Innovation Capabilities Across Industry, Academia, and Research Institutes
Following the gradual phase-out of the Project-Based System (PBS), the government plans to allocate unique missions for each government-funded research institute within this year. To create national representative institutions, common administrative functions such as audits, recruitment, and public relations will be integrated and the technology transfer system will be improved to allow technology royalty revenues generated by these institutes to be utilized as incentives for outstanding employees.
For universities, the government will introduce a block-funding investment approach that allows them to autonomously invest in research personnel and infrastructure. It will also select corporate research institutes with outstanding R&D capabilities in core technologies to encourage corporate R&D activities.
The government will support talented individuals in science, technology, and AI by enhancing economic vitality through entrepreneurship and quality jobs.
– Helping Young Talent to Pursue Dreams in Science, Technology, and AI
To encourage talented individuals to enter and establish themselves in science and engineering fields in Korea, the government will expand gifted education institutions affiliated with institutes of science and technology by establishing two new schools in Chungbuk and Gwangju and converting approximately three existing schools. It will also attract around 600 overseas talents to Korea within this year through support measures including research funding, preferential visa benefits, and improved settlement conditions.
The government will also expand a comprehensive growth and advancement support system covering the entire career cycle from master’s students to doctoral students and early-career researchers. The proportion of master’s and doctoral students receiving scholarships will be increased from the current 1.3% to 2.8% within this year, with the goal of reaching 10% by 2030. Support for basic research among early-career faculty members will also continue to expand, with the goal of reaching a 70% support rate by 2030.
In the AI and AI Transformation (AX) sectors, the government will cultivate highly capable young talent by innovating university AI education through AI-focused universities and establishing AX graduate schools based on industry-academia cooperation.
– Supporting Youth Futures Through Deep-Tech Startups and Job Creation
The government will discover 500+ deep-tech startup teams within this year by strengthening the demonstration and incubation capabilities of institutes of science and technology and government-funded research institutes, including the establishment and expansion of startup centers at institutes of science and technology (from one to four). Institutional improvements will be made to encourage entrepreneurship within institutions, including introducing special provisions for conflicts of interest, and extending startup leave periods at institutes of science and technology.
In particular, to provide intensive support for AI startups, the government will expand public-private joint investment funds to KRW 2 trillion within this year and establish a KRW 20 billion AI venture fund focused on early-stage AI startups. The government will provide an integrated development environment to help young people directly develop AI services and connect outstanding developers with entrepreneurship opportunities through expert consulting.
Above all, the government will create quality jobs to enable young people to pursue stable careers in Korea. It will identify opportunities across various fields, including full-time researchers and postdoctoral researchers at universities, as well as faculty members, researchers, and dedicated support personnel at the four institutes of science and technology and regional branches of government-funded research institutes. It will also create employment opportunities linked to jobs and internships in AI and information security fields.
– Utilizing AI and Science & Technology as Catalysts for Regional Innovation Growth
The government will support regional economic revitalization and a nationwide transformation by promoting AI transformation (AX) of regional industries and utilize R&D as a catalyst for self-sustaining regional growth.
In the second half of 2026, the government will begin establishing AX hubs in four major regions: the southwestern region (mobility and energy), southeastern region (precision manufacturing), Daegu-Gyeongbuk region (bio-healthcare and robotics), and Jeonbuk region (AI factories). Next year, it plans to expand AX nationwide by adding three additional regions: the central region, Gangwon, and Jeju.
At the same time, the government will establish joint AX research institutes between the four institutes of science and technology and companies to provide timely access to core technologies and practical research talent for regional strategic industries. It will also support the employment and entrepreneurship capabilities of young people in non-metropolitan areas by expanding AI innovation education programs outside schools, including the Innovation Academy and AI·SW Maestro, nationwide.
To enable regions to independently develop capabilities they need, the government plans to significantly expand region-led R&D and tentatively allocate approximately three times the previous year’s budget in 2027. It will also establish a dedicated basic research track for early-career researchers in regions and improve systems, including easing R&D matching requirements for regional companies, so that expanded R&D investment can contribute to revitalizing regional R&D ecosystems.
Based on the “Korea Aerospace Industry Promotion Strategy” adopted at the National Space Committee on July 3, the government will implement initiatives to increase the number of aerospace companies to 1,200 and raise Korea’s global market share to 3.0% by 2035.
– Building a Space Highway
In the second half of this year, Korea will successfully complete the fifth launch of the Nuri launch vehicle carrying 15 satellites, including a cluster of small satellites. The government will also advance the development of a reusable next-generation launch vehicle, which aims to reduce launch costs to one-tenth of current levels, and proceed with the selection of a site for the second space center.
– Advancing Toward Becoming a Leading Aerospace Manufacturing Power
In August, the government will launch “Team Korea,” a public-private partnership involving relevant ministries and the private sector, to participate as a key partner from the design phase of the international joint development of next-generation commercial aircraft. The government will also promote the localization of advanced aircraft engines.
– Expanding Lunar Economic Frontiers
In the second half of this year, Korea will launch the Lunar Space Environment Monitor (LUSEM). The government will also proceed without disruption with the launch of a lunar orbit communication satellite in 2029 and a small lunar lander in 2030 to secure the foundation for the future space economy. To strengthen national security and communications sovereignty and create new space and communications markets, Korea will mobilize nationwide capabilities across the government and private sector to establish a Korean low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications network by 2035.
– Establishing the Southern Coast Aerospace Belt
The government will establish Sacheon, where the KASA headquarters is located, as a comprehensive hub for research, manufacturing, and administration (Aerospace Hub), and create a private sector-led innovation ecosystem by connecting Jinju, Changwon, Suncheon, and Goheung.
The Ministry of Science and ICT and KASA will make every effort to ensure that, in an era where securing advanced technologies is directly linked to national survival, policies are implemented swiftly without delay and that the initiatives outlined in the work plans lead to tangible changes experienced by the public rather than remaining only on paper.

title: KASA Aims to Secure Korea’s Future Aircraft Platform by the Early 2030s through Collaboration with Industry
text:
– Aerospace Industry Promotion Strategy Follow-up Measures; KASA Engages with Aircraft System and Component Companies on the Ground
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) held the 8th “Aerospace SOS Meeting” on July 10 (Fri) at KASA headquarters with domestic aircraft system and materials/component companies to discuss the development of hybrid future aircraft. The Aerospace SOS Meeting is a communication channel launched in February to find Speedy, On-site Solutions to the challenges faced by aerospace companies.
A total of 20 companies* involved in the development of aircraft, engines, and materials/components participated in the meeting, which was held to advance future aircraft development outlined in the “Korea Aerospace Industry Promotion Strategy” (hereinafter referred to as the “Industry Promotion Strategy”) announced at the National Space Committee meeting on July 3 (Fri).
* Korea Aerospace Industries, Korean Air, Hyundai Motor Company, Doosan Enerbility, Hyundai Mobis, Hanwha Systems, LIG D&A, Hyundai Wia, Samsung SDI, Next Aerospace, Sambo Motors, KSEP, Kencoa Aerospace, ANH Structure, Hankuk Carbon, DACC Carbon, Hyosung Advanced Materials, SeAH Changwon Integrated Special Steel, Dongyang AK Korea, POSCO Holdings
At the meeting, KASA presented a strategy for division of roles, under which the government will focus on developing hybrid future aircraft that utilize both batteries and engines through government investment, while the private sector will lead the development of fully battery-powered future aircraft.
Under the government-led future aircraft development program, the prototype of a basic hybrid future aircraft is planned to begin flight testing by the end of the 2030s.
In addition, KASA explained the future aircraft development strategy outlined in the Industry Promotion Strategy announced on July 3 and proposed a development approach in which hybrid future aircraft serve as the basic platform, enabling future expansion into public and commercial markets according to mission requirements.
In response, corporate representatives emphasized that expanding participation by domestic materials and components companies is essential for building a future aircraft ecosystem in Korea, and that, above all, new technologies must be developed first through government-led aircraft system development programs. They also proposed the following measures: support for testing and demonstration infrastructure, securing market momentum through the creation of early public demand, and institutional support to expand participation by domestic materials and components companies.
Administrator Oh of KASA emphasized that “securing an independently developed future aircraft platform led by the government is essential for achieving groundbreaking growth in the private aviation industry.” He added, “We will actively collect feedback from domestic private aviation companies and lay the foundation for ensuring that government investment in future aircraft leads to commercialization. Furthermore, we will explore various support measures to secure demand for expanding future aircraft applications into diverse missions, including public services, firefighting, and medical services, and enable their export to global markets.”

title: KASA Strengthens Public-Private Cooperation to Expand Lunar Economic Frontiers
text:
– Commitment to Expanding Support for Industry Announced at the Industry Meeting on Expanding Lunar Economic Frontiers
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) held the “Industry Meeting on Expanding Lunar Economic Frontiers through Public-Private Cooperation” on July 8 (Wed) at the KASA headquarters.
A total of nine companies* developing lunar landers, logistics mobility solutions, and related technologies participated in the meeting. The meeting was particularly significant as it marked the first industry meeting held as a follow-up activity after the National Space Committee approved the “Korea Aerospace Industry Promotion Strategy” (hereinafter referred to as the “Industry Promotion Strategy”) on July 3 (Fri).
* AP Satellite, LIG D&A, MicroInfinity, Intergravity Technologies, Korea Aerospace Industries, Hanwha Systems, Hanwha Aerospace, Hyundai Rotem, Hyundai Motor Company
The meeting was organized to directly hear from domestic companies regarding their detailed R&D progress and plans related to lunar exploration, implement the lunar economy policies outlined in the Industry Promotion Strategy more effectively, and explore practical policy support measures.
The meeting began with opening remarks emphasizing the importance of promoting domestic companies’ entry into the global lunar economy and strengthening government-private sector cooperation to establish a self-sustaining lunar exploration industry ecosystem. It was then followed by a presentation on the development of lunar economic frontiers outlined in the Industry Promotion Strategy and an open discussion.
Prior to the open discussion, Kyungin Kang, Director General of the Space Science Exploration Directorate at KASA, introduced key plans to support domestic companies’ participation in global lunar base development, while enabling them to secure lunar exploration capabilities at an early stage in response to the emerging global lunar economy.
First, Director General Kang explained, “To support the development of private-sector capabilities for building lunar communication infrastructure, we are pursuing a project to develop lunar orbital communication and navigation technologies led by industry starting in 2027, and to launch a demonstration lunar orbital communications satellite (500 kg class) in 2029.”
He also announced plans to support the development and demonstration of small lunar landers (700 kg class) by domestic companies, with the goal of achieving Korea’s first private-sector-led lunar landing in 2030. Through this initiative, KASA aims to help companies establish globally competitive lunar transportation business models at an early stage.
In addition, Director General Kang introduced plans to support projects aimed at enabling Korea’s competitive technologies, including mobility solutions, to become key technologies for global lunar base development. For example, a logistics transportation-focused mobility solution tailored to NASA’s lunar base construction needs will be developed by domestic companies starting in 2028, with a demonstration planned for 2031. Director General stated, “We will continue to identify various policy measures to help domestic companies rapidly transition into global service providers.”
During the following open discussion, company representatives welcomed KASA’s strong commitment to fostering the lunar exploration industry, while sharing practical challenges they face in the field, including difficulties in making initial investments required to enter the global lunar exploration market.
The companies also expressed expectations that strengthened government support as a catalyst would lead to expanded private-sector investment and create a virtuous cycle. They further shared various opinions on policy support measures needed in the field.
Administrator Taeseog Oh stated, “The Moon has now become a key space asset not only from the perspective of science research but also in terms of national security and economic value. Expanding the Republic of Korea’s economic frontier beyond Earth to the Moon and deep space requires the mobilization of national capabilities. In particular, enhancing the competitiveness of industry and actively leveraging its potential capabilities are of utmost importance.”
Administrator Oh also stressed that “this meeting is not a one-time event, but the beginning of continuous and in-depth communication with industry,” adding, “We will establish a strong policy foundation to foster innovative companies such as a ‘Korean SpaceX’ and further strengthen support so that Korean companies can play pivotal roles on the global stage, including NASA’s lunar base development programs.”
Finally, Administrator Oh pledged that KASA would fulfill the role of an “entrepreneurial government” in revitalizing the lunar exploration industry ecosystem, while urging industry to “trust the government and continue investing in the future.”

title: CAS500-4 Satellite Successfully Establishes First Communication After Separation from Launch Vehicle
text:
– Successfully Separated Approximately 2 Hours and 30 Minutes After Launch and Confirmed to be in Good Condition
– First Communication with the Svalbard Ground Station in Norway Successfully Completed at 7:05 p.m. KST on July 7
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh), the Rural Development Administration (Administrator Seungdon Lee), and the Korea Forest Service (Administrator Eun-sik Park) announced that the Next Generation Medium Satellite No. 4 (CAS500-4) was successfully launched at 4:12 p.m. KST on July 7 (Tue) from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, U.S.
Approximately 2 hours and 30 minutes after launch, the CAS500-4 Satellite successfully separated from the launch vehicle at an altitude of about 888 km. About 23 minutes later (approximately 2 hours and 53 minutes after launch), it successfully established its first communication link with the Svalbard Ground Station in Norway at 7:05 p.m. KST. During the initial operation phase, two overseas ground stations (the Svalbard Ground Station in Norway and King Sejong Station in Antarctica) will be utilized.
Through communication with the ground station, KASA confirmed that the CAS500-4 Satellite is in good condition and successfully entered its Sun-synchronous orbit.
With a wide observation swath of 120 km and a resolution of 5 m, the CAS500-4 Satellite is optimized for agricultural observation and forest information monitoring on the Korean Peninsula, enabling it to capture images of the entire country every three days and generate image data.
The CAS500-4 Satellite holds significant importance as it was developed under private sector leadership utilizing the standard platform secured through the development processes of the previous CAS500-1 and CAS500-2 Satellites. Through this project, industry led the entire process from satellite design and manufacturing to testing and verification, further enhancing Korea’s capabilities in the satellite development industry.
Rural Development Administration Administrator Lee stated, “This success marks an important turning point for Korean agriculture as it advances beyond experience and intuition toward data-driven precision agriculture,” adding, “It has opened a new era in which agriculture can be monitored from space based on the national agricultural observation system.” He further emphasized, “By integrating satellite imagery and artificial intelligence (AI), we will further advance crop yield forecasting and agricultural disaster response while realizing digital agriculture that farmers can experience in the field.”
Korea Forest Service Administrator Park stated, “Through the CAS500-4 Satellite, we will rapidly and accurately observe forests to proactively respond to forest disasters such as wildfires and landslides and realize scientific forest management amid the climate crisis.” He added, “As a new starting point for leading the digital and AI transformation of Korea’s forest administration, we will drive tangible changes felt by the public while taking the lead in international cooperation with 121 countries worldwide.”
KASA Administrator Oh stated, “The CAS500-4 Satellite is an important achievement that has expanded private sector-led satellite development capabilities based on a 500 kg-class standard platform.” He added, “By independently securing satellite image data necessary for agriculture, forests, climate, and disaster response, we have significantly strengthened Korea’s competitiveness in private sector-led satellite development and national satellite information utilization capabilities.” He further stated, “We will identify domestic and international demand for satellite launches and further expand the utilization of Korean launch vehicles.”

title: CAS500-4 Satellite Successfully Establishes First Communication with a Korean Ground Station
text:
– First Communication with the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) Ground Station in Daejeon Completed at 10:50 p.m. KST on July 7
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh), the Rural Development Administration (Administrator Seungdon Lee), and the Korea Forest Service (Administrator Eun-sik Park) announced that the Next Generation Medium Satellite No. 4 (CAS500-4) successfully established its first communication link with the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) ground station in Daejeon at 10:50 p.m. KST on July 7, approximately 6 hours and 38 minutes after launch, following three communication links with overseas ground stations. During the initial operation phase, two overseas ground stations (the Svalbard Ground Station in Norway and King Sejong Station in Antarctica) will be utilized.
During the first communication link with the KARI ground station in Daejeon, the deployment of the solar panels and the normal status of the satellite’s main body were confirmed. Additional communication sessions will be conducted to support stable mission operations, including the deployment of the X-band antenna, activation of attitude control system actuators, and functional checks.
Following the initial operation phase, the CAS500-4 Satellite is scheduled to begin full-scale mission operations in 2027 and will provide data for agricultural and forest observation, as well as disaster and emergency response areas such as wildfires.

title: Korea’s Next-Generation Medium Satellite No. 4 (CAS500-4) to Launch on July 7 (Tue) at around 4 p.m.
text:
– Launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in the U.S. to an 888 km Sun-synchronous Orbit
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh), the Rural Development Administration (Administrator Seungdon Lee), and the Korea Forest Service (Administrator Eun-sik Park) announced that the Next Generation Medium Satellite No. 4 (CAS500-4) will be launched at 4:10 p.m. KST on July 7 (Tue) from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, U.S.
CAS500-4 has successfully completed all pre-launch preparations, including functional checks and propellant fueling, over the past approximately 30 days at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The satellite is currently mounted on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket and awaiting launch.
Approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes after launch, CAS500-4 will separate from the launch vehicle. About 31 minutes later (approximately 2 hours and 53 minutes after launch), it is scheduled to establish its first communication link with the Svalbard Ground Station in Norway. This communication will confirm whether the satellite has successfully entered its target orbit.
Equipped with a payload developed using Korea’s core technologies, CAS500-4 will be capable of capturing images of the entire country every three days using its wide-area observation camera. The satellite is expected to be utilized in various fields, including agricultural and forest management, forest change monitoring, disaster and emergency response, climate change analysis, and enhancement of public safety.
Following launch, CAS500-4 will undergo an initial operation phase of approximately four months in an orbit at an altitude of about 888 km and is scheduled to begin full-scale mission operations in the first half of 2027.
The launch of CAS500-4 will be broadcast live through KASA’s YouTube channel (https://www.youtube.com/@kasamedia) and other platforms such as Korea’s Naver CHZZK.

title: K-Space Industry Showcases Reliability and Capabilities in Eastern Europe
text:
– Space Public-Private Delegation Holds “Space Day” Eventsin Romania (July 1) and Poland (July 3)
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA, Minister Cho Hyun) held “Space Day” events in Bucharest, Romania, on July 1 (Wed) and Warsaw, Poland, on July 3 (Fri), respectively, to strengthen space cooperation with local government agencies and private companies.
Organized by the Space Public-Private Delegation composed of KASA, MOFA, and major Korean space companies (Head of Delegation: Jun-shik Hwang, Director-General for Climate, Environment and Science Diplomacy at MOFA), the events featured presentations by the two countries’ space agencies on their respective space policy directions, as well as introductions of Korean companies’ technological capabilities and willingness to cooperate. The events also included one-on-one networking sessions, providing opportunities for Korean companies to discuss specific cooperation opportunities with local organizations and companies.
The Korea-Romania Space Day, which began with opening remarks by Mihnea Costoiu, Rector of the National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest, and MOFA Director-General Hwang, was attended by nine Korean companies* and representatives from major space and security related government agencies, institutions, and companies, including the Romanian Space Agency (ROSA), the Ministry of National Defence (MApN), and the National Research Authority (ANCSI). The Romanian government expressed strong expectations for future Korea-Romania space cooperation through welcoming remarks by Andrei Alexandru, President of ANCSI, and Daniel Eugeniu Crunteanu, President of ROSA.
* Korean space companies: Nara Space, Satrec Initiative, Space Liintech, Spacebeam, Innospace, Kairos Space, Telepix, Hanwha Systems, Hyundai Rotem
In addition, Jeonghoon Kim, Director of International Affairs Division at KASA, and Oana Cojeanu, Director of International Cooperation at ROSA, introduced the space policies and ecosystems of both countries, while participating Korean companies presented their specialized capabilities and cooperation ideas. The advanced satellite solutions presented by Korean companies, including satellite systems and Earth observation technologies, closely matched Romania’s defense modernization needs and attracted significant interest from local government and military officials. Romanian private space companies also introduced their respective technological capabilities and cooperation proposals, seeking opportunities for technological collaboration with the Korean delegation. Following the presentations, one on one meetings and networking sessions enabled Korean companies to directly engage with Romanian government agencies and military officials gathered at the event, discussing potential business opportunities and cooperation plans.
Meanwhile, the Korea-Poland Space Day held in Warsaw was attended by 12 Korean companies* and senior officials from major space and security related institutions, including the Polish Space Agency (POLSA), the Ministry of Economic Development and Technology, and the Ministry of National Defence. Beginning with welcoming remarks by Marta Ewa Wachowicz, President of POLSA, and Director-General Hwang at MOFA, as well as congratulatory remarks by Andrzej Domanski, Minister of Economic Development and Technology, the two countries explored opportunities for technological cooperation in line with the NewSpace era led by the private sector. In addition, Tae Jun-youl, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Poland, and Bartosz Wisniewski, Ambassador of Poland to the Republic of Korea, attended the event together and delivered welcoming remarks, emphasizing both countries’ commitment to expanding cooperation in the space sector.
* Korean space companies: Nara Space, Delta V Solutions, Satrec Initiative, Space Liintech, Spacebeam, Uzuro Tech, Innospace, Kairos Space, Telepix, Korea Aerospace Industries, Hanwha Systems, Hyundai Rotem
The two sides then presented their space policies and international cooperation initiatives, while Korean space companies provided briefings on specialized technologies, including satellite development and data utilization. Subsequent sessions featured presentations on Korea’s space policies and roadmap, followed by introductions of Korean companies’ launch vehicle and component technologies. Through one-on-one meetings and networking sessions, Korean companies engaged in in-depth discussions with Polish government officials, while representatives from leading Polish space companies and institutions also participated to facilitate further dialogue.
The Space Day events, jointly organized by KASA and MOFA in Belgium (June 29), Romania (July 1), and Poland (July 3), are expected to strengthen space cooperation with the EU, NATO, and major European countries while providing a stepping stone for Korean space companies’ entry into the European market. In particular, the events served as an opportunity to identify the potential for expanding the trust and achievements established by K-Defense in the Eastern European market into the space sector. The government plans to continue expanding opportunities for international cooperation in response to Korean space companies’ demand for entry into new markets.

title: KASA Hears from Satellite Imagery Pioneers Creating New Value-Added Services
text:
– Gathering Feedback on Challenges Faced by Satellite Imagery Companies and Discussing Support Measures
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) listened to the opinions of companies and discussed support measures to promote the growth of Korea’s satellite imagery industry at an industry meeting held on June 30 (Tue) at the ITX conference room at Yongsan Station.
The meeting was organized to assess market conditions for the domestic and global satellite imagery utilization industries and discuss ways to expand the use of services provided by domestic satellite imagery companies.
Fifteen companies specializing in satellite imagery participated in the event: KT SAT, Gaia3D, Nara Space, Lumir, Meissa, Satrec Initiative, SI Analytics, SIIS, UST21, Innopam, Contec, Telepix, Korea Aerospace Industries, InSpace, and Hanwha Systems.
“Through this meeting, we will strengthen communication with domestic satellite imagery companies and strive to ensure that the government plays a meaningful role in supporting the satellite imagery utilization industry, which is growing under private sector leadership,” said Administrator Oh of KASA.

title: Korea’s Space Sector Joins as One Team to Advance Development of Reusable Next-Generation Launch Vehicle
text:
– Industry-Academia-Research Stakeholders Gather to Ensure the Success of the 2032 Lunar Lander Launch Mission and Secure Reusable Launch Vehicle Technologies
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) held the “Industry-Academia-Research Meeting on Advancing the Development of the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle” on June 30 (Tue) at the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) to ensure the successful development of the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle, which is being developed as Korea’s main space launch vehicle for the 2030s.
The meeting was organized as a platform for consolidating the capabilities of industry, academia, and research institutions at the point when the system conceptual design process was being completed, following the transition of the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle development program toward a reusable launch vehicle similar to SpaceX’s Falcon 9.
Approximately 70 participants attended the meeting, including representatives from KARI, the lead research and development institution, Hanwha Aerospace, the system integration company, and other participating companies such as HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hyundai Rotem, Vitzro Nextech, Hanyang ENG, as well as domestic expert advisors from industry, academia, and research sectors.
During the meeting, KASA and the other participants shared the development status and detailed schedules for each component of the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle, as well as the progress of lunar lander development. They also discussed measures to develop a competitive launch vehicle for the 2030s and successfully accomplish lunar exploration missions.
In particular, officials in charge of the Phase 2 Lunar Exploration Program (lunar lander development) also attended the meeting to share the current status and development plans of the program. This strengthened communication between the two projects and enabled discussions on cooperation measures to successfully accomplish the 2032 lunar landing mission.
* To achieve independent space exploration capabilities, Korea plans to develop the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle and independently launch a lunar lander in 2032. (Launch vehicle performance verification vehicle in 2031; lunar soft-landing verification vehicle and lunar lander in 2032)
“Amid the beginning of the space economy era, accelerated by developments such as SpaceX’s initial public offering (IPO), the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle, being developed as Korea’s main launch vehicle for the 2030s, will serve as a key pillar not only in dramatically enhancing Korea’s independent access to space capabilities but also in building a space highway for low-cost, high-frequency launches,” said Administrator Oh of KASA. “Through this meeting, we will bring together national capabilities and ensure the successful development of the Next-Generation Launch Vehicle without disruption.”

title: KASA Announces Guidelines for Private Sector Use of the Naro Space Center
text:
– Guidelines Include Consultation Procedures, Fee Calculation Criteria, and Safety Control Measures
– Expected to Enable First Commercial Launch by a Private Launch Vehicle Company Using a Domestic Launch Site
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) announced the full opening of the Naro Space Center to the private sector on June 29 (Mon) and released the “Guidelines for Private Sector Use of the Naro Space Center” (hereinafter referred to as the “Guidelines”) through the KASA website (www.kasa.go.kr) and the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) website (www.kari.re.kr).
The Guidelines specify procedures and fee criteria for private companies’ use of the Naro Space Center’s facilities, equipment, and services, including four-step consultation procedures, fee calculation methods, plans for establishing the Private Launch Safety Control Council, and safety and security guidelines.
In particular, reflecting feedback collected through meetings with private companies and expert consultations, the Guidelines include measures to reduce the burden on companies and improve accessibility, such as applying fee discounts based on company size. These measures are expected to reduce the costs and procedural burdens faced by Korean companies that have previously relied on overseas or offshore launch sites. In addition, private companies are expected to gain the foundation to carry out the entire lifecycle of launch vehicle development, from testing stages to commercial launches, at a domestic launch site.
Meanwhile, KASA plans to open private launch sites (currently being constructed within the Naro Space Center to enable private companies to conduct launches in Korea) in phases, divided into Stage 1 (third quarter of 2027) and Stage 2 (first quarter of 2031). Upon completion of Stage 2 construction, additional assembly and testing facilities capable of supporting launch vehicle assembly and payload testing will be established, further expanding the scope of private companies’ use of the Naro Space Center.
“Beyond simply opening national facilities, the Guidelines represent a significant step toward strengthening the support system for the private sector in the space industry,” said Administrator Oh of KASA. “Through these efforts, we will continue to provide support to ensure the stable establishment of a private-sector led commercial space ecosystem.”

title: Korea-EU-NATO Space Day Held
text:
– Discussions on Cooperation with Space, Security, and Policy Stakeholders and Opportunities for Business Engagement
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA, Administrator Taeseog Oh) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA, Minister Cho Hyun) held the “Korea-EU-NATO Space Day” event on June 29 (Mon) in Brussels, Belgium, to strengthen cooperation with the European Union (EU) and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in the space sector.
Organized by the Korea Space Public-Private Delegation, composed of KASA, MOFA, and Korean space companies (headed by Jun-shik Hwang, Director-General for Climate, Environment and Science Diplomacy at MOFA), the event served as an opportunity to advance cooperation in security, defense, and science and technology agreed upon at the 11th Korea-EU Summit held on June 10.
Attended by approximately 80 participants, including relevant Korean institutions and 12 Korean space companies*, as well as nine EU and NATO organizations** and local institutions, companies, and associations, the event was successfully held with the aim of strengthening cooperation between relevant space organizations from both sides and supporting Korean space companies’ expansion into overseas markets.
* Nara Space, Delta V Solutions, Unmanned Exploration Research Institute, Satrec Initiative, Space Liin Tech, Spacebeam, Uzuro Tech, Innospace, Kairospace, Telepix, Hyundai Rotem, and Hyundai Motor Company
** EU: DG DEFIS, EEAS, EDA, ESA, SEDE, ESPI / NATO: NATO HQ (Defence Industry, Innovation and Armaments Division, Defence Policy and Planning Division), Allied Command, and NSPA
Participating Korean companies introduced their specialized capabilities and cooperation proposals in areas including launch vehicles, satellite development, satellite imagery analysis, data utilization, and space equipment, materials, and medicine. The event also provided an opportunity to highlight the capabilities and potential of Korea’s space industry, with the attendance of major local media outlets.
Various sessions were held on site to deepen strategic cooperation between the two sides while creating tangible business opportunities for Korean companies. During the High-Level Dialogue Session, participants discussed mid- and long-term cooperation plans in the space domain with EU and NATO officials. In the Panel Discussion Session, participants exchanged views in depth on ways to establish practical partnerships, including in satellite communications and the utilization of Earth observation data, based on the technologies and cooperation proposals introduced by Korean companies. A Networking Reception held following the event provided opportunities for more informal discussions, while Korean companies held one-on-one meetings with representatives from major European government organizations to explore opportunities for participation in European multilateral cooperation programs and entry into global supply chains.
“Recent geopolitical conflicts have reaffirmed the importance of space infrastructure, including satellite communications and Earth observation, from a security perspective,” said Director-General Jun-shik Hwang at MOFA. “Based on their advanced technological and manufacturing capabilities, Korean space companies will be able to contribute to strengthening Europe’s space capabilities and become trusted partners.”
“This event was a meaningful opportunity for Korea’s innovative space companies to directly communicate with key European space organizations, understand local industry trends, and lay the groundwork for cooperation,” said Hong-tae Jang, Planning and Coordination Officer at KASA. “Based on the networks established through this event, we will actively support the realization of practical cooperation among private companies in the future.”
The Korea-EU-NATO Space Day is assessed to have strengthened space and security cooperation with Europe and is expected to serve as a practical stepping stone toward Korean space companies’ entry into European supply chains. Based on the outcomes of this event, the government plans to continue expanding cooperation opportunities, such as this event, in line with Korean companies’ demands for entering new markets.

title: KASA to Dispatch a Space Public-Private Delegation to the EU, NATO, and Eastern Europe
text:
